p: (1) The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script.
The form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals.

(2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (1), for a period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, the English language shall continue to be used for all the official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before such commencement:

Provided that the President may, during the said period, by order{1} authorise the use of the Hindi language in addition to the English language and of the Devanagari form of numerals in addition to the international form of Indian numerals for any of the official purposes of the Union.
(3) Notwithstanding anything in this article, Parliament may by law provide for the use, after the said period of fifteen years, of—
(a) the English language; or
(b) the Devanagari form of numerals,
for such purposes as may be specified in the law.
343.s: Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union, using the international form of Indian numerals. English was to continue for official Union purposes for fifteen years, and Parliament can by law allow English or Devanagari numerals after that.
k: use of english for official purposes

p: (1) The President shall, at the expiration of five years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of ten years from such commencement, by order constitute a Commission which shall consist of a Chairman and such other members representing the different languages specified in the Eighth Schedule as the President may appoint, and the order shall define the procedure to be followed by the Commission.
(2) It shall be the duty of the Commission to make recommendations to the President as to—
(a) the progressive use of the Hindi language for the official purposes of the Union;
(b) restrictions on the use of the English language for all or any of the official purposes of the Union;
(c) the language to be used for all or any of the purposes mentioned in article 348;
(d) the form of numerals to be used for any one or more specified purposes of the Union;

(e) any other matter referred to the Commission by the President as regards the official language of the Union and the language for communication between the Union and a State or between one State and another and their use.

(3) In making their recommendations under clause (2), the Commission shall have due regard to the industrial, cultural and scientific advancement of India, and the just claims and the interests of persons belonging to the non-Hindi speaking areas in regard to the public services.

(4) There shall be constituted a Committee consisting of thirty members, of whom twenty shall be members of the House of the People and ten shall be members of the Council of States to be elected respectively by the members of the House of the People and the members of the Council of States in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
(5) It shall be the duty of the Committee to examine the recommendations of the Commission constituted under clause (1) and to report to the President their opinion thereon.
(6) Notwithstanding anything in article 343, the President may, after consideration of the report referred to in clause (5), issue directions in accordance with the whole or any part of that report.
344.s: The President had to set up a Commission five and ten years after the Constitution began to recommend wider use of Hindi, limits on English and related matters, respecting non-Hindi speakers' interests in public services. A committee of 20 House of the People and 10 Council of States members reviews its advice, and the President can then issue directions.

p: Subject to the provisions of articles 346 and 347, the Legislature of a State may by law adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the State or Hindi as the language or languages to be used for all or any of the official purposes of that State:

Provided that, until the Legislature of the State otherwise provides by law, the English language shall continue to be used for those official purposes within the State for which it was being used immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.
345.s: A State Legislature can, by law, adopt one or more languages used in the State, or Hindi, for the State's official purposes. Until it does, English continues for the official purposes it was used for before the Constitution began.
k: can a state choose its language

p: The language for the time being authorised for use in the Union for official purposes shall be the official language for communication between one State and another State and between a State and the Union:
Provided that if two or more States agree that the Hindi language should be the official language for communication between such States, that language may be used for such communication.
346.s: The language currently authorised for the Union's official purposes is used for communication between States and between a State and the Union. Two or more States can agree to use Hindi between themselves.

p: On a demand being made in that behalf the President may, if he is satisfied that a substantial proportion of the population of a State desire the use of any language spoken by them to be recognised by that State, direct that such language shall also be officially recognised throughout that State or any part thereof for such purpose as he may specify.
347.s: If a substantial part of a State's population demands it, the President can direct that a language they speak also be officially recognised throughout the State or part of it, for purposes the President specifies.
k: recognition of minority language in state
language spoken by section of population

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, until Parliament by law otherwise provides—
(a) all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court;
(b) the authoritative texts—
(i) of all Bills to be introduced or amendments thereto to be moved in either House of Parliament or in the House or either House of the Legislature of a State;
(ii) of all Acts passed by Parliament or the Legislature of a State and of all Ordinances promulgated by the President or the Governor {1}*** of a State; and
(iii) of all orders, rules, regulations and bye-laws issued under this Constitution or under any law made by Parliament or the Legislature of a State,
shall be in the English language.

(2) Notwithstanding anything in sub-clause (a) of clause (1), the Governor {1}*** of a State may, with the previous consent of the President, authorise the use of the Hindi language, or any other language used for any official purposes of the State, in proceedings in the High Court having its principal seat in that State:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to any judgment, decree or order passed or made by such High Court.

(3) Notwithstanding anything in sub-clause (b) of clause (1), where the Legislature of a State has prescribed any language other than the English language for use in Bills introduced in, or Acts passed by, the Legislature of the State or in Ordinances promulgated by the Governor {2}*** of the State or in any order, rule, regulation or bye-law referred to in paragraph (iii) of that sub-clause, a translation of the same in the English language published under the authority of the Governor {2}*** of the State in the Official Gazette of that State shall be deemed to be the authoritative text thereof in the English language under this article.
f: The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
348.s: Until Parliament provides otherwise, Supreme Court and High Court proceedings and the authoritative texts of Bills, Acts, Ordinances, rules and orders are in English. A Governor, with the President's consent, can allow Hindi or a State language in High Court proceedings, except judgments, decrees and orders, and an official English translation counts for State laws made in another language.

p: During the period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, no Bill or amendment making provision for the language to be used for any of the purposes mentioned in clause (1) of article 348 shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament without the previous sanction of the President, and the President shall not give his sanction to the introduction of any such Bill or the moving of any such amendment except after he has taken into consideration the recommendations of the Commission constituted under clause (1) of article 344 and the report of the Committee constituted under clause (4) of that article.
349.s: A rule for the first fifteen years after the Constitution began: a Bill or amendment in Parliament on the language of courts and laws needed the President's prior sanction. The President could give it only after considering the Official Language Commission's recommendations and the parliamentary committee's report.

p: Every person shall be entitled to submit a representation for the redress of any grievance to any officer or authority of the Union or a State in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State, as the case may be.
350.s: Every person can submit a request to fix a grievance to any Union or State officer or authority in any language used in the Union or in that State.
k: right to petition in any language

p: It shall be the endeavour of every State and of every local authority within the State to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups; and the President may issue such directions to any State as he considers necessary or proper for securing the provision of such facilities.
f: Arts. 350A and 350B ins. by s.21., ibid. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
350A.s: Every State and local authority must try to provide adequate teaching in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minority groups. The President can give States directions to ensure these facilities.

p: (1) There shall be a Special Officer for linguistic minorities to be appointed by the President.

(2) It shall be the duty of the Special Officer to investigate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for linguistic minorities under this Constitution and report to the President upon those matters at such intervals as the President may direct, and the President shall cause all such reports to be laid before each House of Parliament, and sent to the Governments of the States concerned.]
350B.s: The President appoints a Special Officer for linguistic minorities, who investigates matters about their constitutional safeguards and reports to the President. These reports are laid before each House of Parliament and sent to the State Governments concerned.

p: It shall be the duty of the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language, to develop it so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all the elements of the composite culture of India and to secure its enrichment by assimilating without interfering with its genius, the forms, style and expressions used in Hindustani and in the other languages of India specified in the Eighth Schedule, and by drawing, wherever necessary or desirable, for its vocabulary, primarily on Sanskrit and secondarily on other languages.
351.s: The Union must promote the spread and development of Hindi so it can express all parts of India's composite culture. It should enrich Hindi with forms and expressions from Hindustani and other Eighth Schedule languages, drawing vocabulary mainly from Sanskrit and then from other languages.

why: Minerva Mills (1980) held that abrogating Articles 14 and 19 for a class of laws destroys the basic structure; Coelho (2007) treats the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the test for Ninth Schedule laws.
Coelho (2007) called Article 32 "an important and integral part of the basic structure", and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under it cannot be ousted.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the High Courts' power of judicial review under Article 226, and their superintendence under Article 227, are part of the inviolable basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot amend this article to make its power unlimited.

The NJAC case (2015) struck down the Ninety-ninth Amendment's new method of appointing judges as a breach of judicial independence, so the core of how judges are appointed is part of the basic structure.
Names India as a Union of States. Abolishing the Union or the States would undo federalism and India's sovereignty, both part of the framework.
This is the hook for testing laws against fundamental rights. Courts have said the power to test legislation "can never be ousted".
Core guarantees against discrimination and untouchability. Coelho (2007) named Article 15 among the rights forming part of the basic structure.
Freedom of religion is the main textual home of secularism, which the Court has repeatedly called a basic feature.
Judicial review by the High Courts, held to be basic, depends on the High Courts existing.
Adult suffrage is the foundation of democracy and free and fair elections.
Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held that the part of the Preamble relating to the basic structure cannot be amended; Balram Singh (2024) upheld adding "socialist" and "secular".
Defines "the State" against which fundamental rights are enforced; gutting it would hollow out the rights.
Equality of opportunity in public employment is part of the equality code, though clauses on reservation have been changed and upheld.
Basic protections of personal liberty and fair criminal process, closely tied to Article 21.
Bans on forced labour and child labour in hazardous work relate to human dignity; no case has tested their repeal.
Religious freedom of groups and the bar on State religious instruction carry secularism into practice.
Minority rights to culture and to run educational institutions support pluralism and secularism.
The Directive to separate the judiciary from the executive expresses separation of powers and judicial independence.
An elected President as head of state is part of the republican form of government.
How the President is elected. Entrenched: changing it needs ratification by half the States.
Extent of Union executive power, one half of the federal balance. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
Ministers advise the President and answer collectively to the Lok Sabha: the core of parliamentary government.
An elected Parliament, with the States represented in it. Representation of the States is entrenched.
Fixed terms for the Houses guarantee periodic elections.
Parliament cannot discuss a judge's conduct except on a motion for removal, a rule tied to judicial independence.
Judges' salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage while in office, a guard on judicial independence.
Courts of record with power to punish contempt, part of the courts' ability to make their orders effective.
The Supreme Court settles disputes between the Union and the States, a federal safeguard.
Special leave to appeal lets the Supreme Court correct any court or tribunal, central to access to justice.
Each State has its own executive, part of the federal structure.
Extent of State executive power. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
State ministers advise the Governor and answer to the Assembly: parliamentary government at State level.
An elected State Legislature with fixed terms, needed for both democracy and federalism.
Transfers of High Court judges. The NJAC case struck down the 2014 change to this article as part of the same scheme.
High Court control over the subordinate courts keeps the district judiciary independent of the executive.
The division of law-making power between Parliament and the States. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
No tax without the authority of law, a basic rule-of-law guarantee.
An independent Election Commission conducts elections; without it free and fair elections would be at risk.
A single electoral roll with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
The right to education. Its insertion was upheld, but no case says whether removing it would breach the basic structure.
The welfare-state directives most closely tied to the balance between Parts III and IV. Removing them might upset that balance; untested.
Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedure. Touches both separation of powers and judicial review.
Binding precedent and the power to do complete justice. Important to the Court's role, but not tested as basic.
An independent auditor of public accounts supports the rule of law and accountability; untested.
Organisational rules for the High Courts. Some core is needed for judicial review, but the details can change.
President's Rule. Its use is reviewable (Bommai), and abuse can damage federalism and democracy, but the article itself is not part of the basic structure.
Suspension of rights during emergency. Since 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; widening this power again could touch the essence of rights.
Parliament already changes State boundaries by ordinary law; the federal structure survives individual changes.
Citizenship rules. Parliament already controls citizenship by law under Article 11.
These shield certain laws from fundamental rights challenges. Removing them would restore rights, not damage the structure.
Powers to adapt or restrict rights for armed forces and martial law; administrative in nature.
Individual Directive Principles. The balance between Parts III and IV is basic, but no single directive has been held essential.
Fundamental duties were added in 1976 and are not enforceable in court.
Detailed rules on the President, Vice-President and conduct of business. Can change without touching a basic feature.
Detailed rules on Parliament's membership, officers and procedure.
Legislative and financial procedure, and ordinances. Can be redesigned without damaging democracy itself.
Organisation and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court beyond its core review power. Many have been amended before.
Form and reporting of public accounts.
Detailed rules on Governors and State executive business.
Detailed rules on State Legislatures, their officers and members.
State legislative and financial procedure, assent to Bills and ordinances.
Detailed rules on High Court judges and jurisdiction beyond the core review power.
Appointment and rules for district judges and subordinate courts.
How Union territories are governed. Parliament has changed this often.
Panchayats, added in 1992. Local democracy, but not part of the original framework or any holding.
Administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Specific rules within the division of legislative power. Entrenched where in Chapter I of Part XI, but individually changeable.
Administrative relations between the Union and the States.
Distribution of revenues and the Finance Commission. Revised many times, including by GST in 2016.
Freedom of trade within India and its exceptions.
Civil services and Public Service Commissions.
Tribunals may exist; what is part of the basic structure is the High Courts' and Supreme Court's review over them, not these articles.
Election law-making and the bar on courts during elections.
Reservations in legislatures and services, commissions and lists. Many have sunset clauses or have been amended; upheld when changed.
Linguistic minority protections and the Hindi directive.
Emergency powers. The articles themselves are not part of the basic structure.
Transitional provisions continuing earlier laws, courts and officers.
The right to property. Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held it is not part of the basic structure.
Temporary and special provisions for particular States. Several have been changed or abrogated and upheld.
Abolition of titles. An equality measure, but minor; no case suggests it is essential.
Equal justice and free legal aid, the directive most closely tied to effective access to justice.
Concurrent power over GST, added in 2016. A specific fiscal arrangement within federalism.
Interpretation clause for the Part on finance.
Co-operative societies, added in 2011. Detailed regulatory rules.
Salaries of members and rules of procedure and language in Parliament.
Definitions, interpretation, short title, commencement, the Hindi text and repeals.
Lists the States and Union territories. Parliament changes it by ordinary law under Articles 3 and 4.
Salaries and allowances of constitutional office-holders.
Forms of oaths, including the oath to uphold the Constitution.
Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Entrenched, but the numbers change by amendment.
Autonomous districts in the North-East; amended many times.
The Union, State and Concurrent Lists as a scheme are the core of federalism. Individual entries are changed often.
Laws shielded from fundamental rights challenges. Removing the shield would not damage the structure.
The anti-defection law, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan. Repealing it would not breach a basic feature.

amend.s: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot use that power to destroy its identity or make the power unlimited.

jr.s: The High Courts and the Supreme Court must be able to test laws and government action against the Constitution.

indep.s: Judges must be appointed and kept in office free of control by the executive.

rol.c: P. Sambamurthy (1986); I.R. Coelho (2007); Raj Narain (1975)
rol.s: Government acts under law, and its decisions can be tested by independent courts.

equality.t: Equality and the essence of fundamental rights
equality.s: The core of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and the essence of each fundamental right, cannot be abrogated.

balance.t: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
balance.s: Parts III and IV must be kept in harmony; neither may be made to swallow the other.

democracy.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
democracy.s: Government by elected representatives, with an elected head of state.

elections.s: Elections must be free and fair, and their results open to lawful challenge.

secular.c: S.R. Bommai (1994); I.R. Coelho (2007); Balram Singh (2024)
secular.s: The State treats all religions equally and has no religion of its own.

federal.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
federal.s: Power is divided between the Union and the States, and the States are not mere agents of the Centre.

sop.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); I.R. Coelho (2007); Presidential Reference on assent to Bills (2025)
sop.s: Legislature, executive and judiciary each keep their own sphere.

supremacy.s: Every organ of the State is bound by the Constitution.

sovereign.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
sovereign.s: India is a sovereign Union; its unity and integrity are part of the framework.

parl.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
parl.s: Ministers are drawn from and answerable to an elected legislature.

access.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
access.s: People must be able to reach a court to enforce their rights.
